name: Unique Transformation
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] I went from [comparable before measure] to [after measure] in [period]. Without [verified omitted resource or method].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I went from six hours to four hours per weekly draft in one month. Without hiring an editor.
requirements: Verify writer identity, comparable baseline and endpoint, period, and absence of the named resource. Explain other changes and measurement limits. The omitted method and the outcome do not establish causation.

name: Failure Story
template: [Only with source-backed writer observations; otherwise label hypothetical] I saw [bounded group] attempt [ambitious action] in [period]. [Documented setback] followed.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I saw two pilot teams try to replace their review process in a week. Both restored manual review after missing required checks.
requirements: Verify observation, group size, action, period and setback. Any proportion needs its denominator and source. Do not turn a small sample into an industry failure rate or invent client experience.

name: Make People Feel Seen
template: If you are [audience with stated goal], but [documented obstacle], this [specific resource] is for you.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: If you are a founder trying to organize customer interviews, but your notes are scattered across documents, this review checklist is for you.
requirements: Use an audience and obstacle supported by the brief or research. Do not infer sensitive traits or prescribe feelings. Deliver the promised resource.

name: Strong Disagreement
template: [Only with the writer's supplied position] [Attributed exact quote or clearly labeled paraphrase]. I disagree about [specific point], because [supported reason].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Fictional workshop claim: Every draft should be published immediately. I disagree about skipping review when a draft contains customer quotes.
requirements: Obtain the writer's disagreement. Verify the quote and attribution; preserve quoted spans exactly. Label paraphrases. Address the actual claim without inventing a speaker or attributing this synthetic example to a real person.

name: Opinion as Fact
template: [Evidence-backed scoped claim, or explicitly labeled opinion]. Here is the [evidence or reasoning] behind it.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: In this fictional ten-draft review, unsupported numbers caused six rejections. Here is what the review recorded.
requirements: Keep the historical structure name only. Never promote an opinion to fact. Supply evidence, dates, scope and denominators for factual claims, or identify whose opinion it is and obtain their supplied position. No invented forecasts or revenue lifts.

name: Rebellion Story
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] I was told [exact advice or labeled paraphrase]. I chose [different action]. [Documented outcome] followed.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I was told to wait until the entire guide was ready. I tested one section first. Three reviewers identified the same missing step.
requirements: Verify the advice, writer's choice and outcome. Use quotation marks only for exact sourced wording. Do not imply that ignoring advice caused success or that competitors fell behind without evidence.

name: Trigger FOMO
template: [Only with the writer's supplied recommendation] I would recommend [method] for [specific situation], with [important limit]. Here is the [supported benefit or proposed test].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I would recommend a shared review queue for teams losing track of approvals, provided someone owns the queue. Here is a one-week test.
requirements: Preserve selective recommendation, not manufactured scarcity. Ground fit and limits in the brief and evidence. Distinguish measured outcomes from proposed benefits. No guaranteed gains or invented exclusion.

name: Contrarian Post
template: You can be [positive trait or achievement] and still face [specific evidenced limitation]. [Writer's supplied challenge or recommendation].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: A team can publish regularly and still miss required source checks. Review the evidence behind each claim before increasing output.
requirements: Support the limitation and obtain any opinion attributed to the writer. Do not invent the reader's income, behavior or shortcomings. Explain when the challenge applies and avoid unsupported loss estimates.

name: Set a Goal, Show Your Process
template: Hypothetical plan: If I wanted to [goal] within [proposed period], I would try [process], checking [success measure].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Hypothetical plan: If I wanted to test a customer-interview guide in two weeks, I would run one rehearsal and revise the questions before recruiting more reviewers.
requirements: Label the goal and process hypothetical. Explain assumptions, resources and feasibility. A proposed deadline is not a promise or achieved result. Do not imply a track record.

name: Subject Masterclass
template: A [verified reading or viewing duration] lesson on [topic]. [If sourced and authorized: how a customer achieved a bounded result in a measured period; otherwise: the specific method taught].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: A two-minute lesson on reviewing generated summaries. Follow one fictional customer team's checks for missing quotes and unsupported numbers.
requirements: Check that the lesson fits the stated duration and delivers its topic. Customer identity, permission to disclose, result, baseline and period need evidence. Otherwise teach the method without a customer success claim.

name: Golden Advice
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] I [tested or taught a verified scope] over [period]. Here are [supported findings].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I tested four interview-note formats over two weeks. Here are the fields reviewers used and the ones they skipped.
requirements: Verify participation, count, period and records behind each finding. Preserve both testing and teaching variants when relevant. Do not inflate counts, invent trainees or imply consistent results without comparable observations.

name: Leverage FOFU
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] I encountered [specific advice] about [subject]. Here is why it is risky under [conditions].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I encountered advice to publish generated customer quotes without checking the transcript. Here is how that can misattribute a statement.
requirements: Source the encounter and quote or label a paraphrase. Explain a supported failure mechanism. Use a worst-ranking only with a defined comparison set and criteria; otherwise retain the concrete warning. No invented personal experience.

name: Quantified Strategy/Framework
template: [Only with source-backed and disclosure-approved client evidence; otherwise label hypothetical] After [client] used [framework], [measured result] changed by [amount] over [period]. Here is the process and what else changed.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: After a fictional client added a review checklist, average revision time fell from 50 to 40 minutes over four weeks. The team also reduced article length.
requirements: Verify relationship, permission, baseline, measure, amount, period and records. State what else changed and distinguish observed association from attributable savings or revenue. Report gross versus net and one-time versus recurring values accurately.

name: Personalized Result
template: [Only with source-backed and disclosure-approved client evidence; otherwise label hypothetical] Here is how [specific client] approached [goal] and recorded [bounded outcome] within [period].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Here is how a fictional consultancy piloted an interview-summary service and completed its first three paid projects within two months.
requirements: Verify the client relationship, outcome, timeframe, scope and permission. Explain the process without claiming it guarantees replication. Do not convert a partial automation or first sale into a fully automated business or recurring revenue.

name: Expert's First-Time Approach
template: Hypothetical teaching approach: If I were helping [audience] attempt [goal] for the first time, I would start with [step]. Here is the full proposed process.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Hypothetical teaching approach: If I were helping a founder run a first customer interview, I would start with one question about a recent event. Here is the proposed process.
requirements: Label the approach hypothetical. Do not infer expertise or credentials from the historical structure name. Support factual guidance, name assumptions and deliver the promised breakdown.

name: Before-After Transformation
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] I went from [before situation] to [after situation] over [period]. These are the changes recorded along the way.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I went from separate interview notes to a shared review log over six weeks. These are the changes recorded along the way.
requirements: Verify the writer's before and after states and period. Use comparable measures for quantified changes. Separate process changes from demonstrated causes of the outcome. Do not invent a learning journey or business history.

name: Target Audience Problem/Growth
template: In [dated bounded source], [specific audience] reported [problem or improvement]. Here is [supported explanation or clearly labeled hypothesis].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: In a fictional September interview set, four of six founders reported losing track of unanswered customer questions. Here are the situations they described.
requirements: Provide dated sources, sample selection and scope. Distinguish reported experience from verified performance. Current language requires current evidence. Do not generalize a few reports to all founders or present an explanatory hypothesis as causation.

name: Problem-Agitate (PAS)
template: [Sourced audience or sample] faces [specific problem]. Here are [actual count] parts of the problem and [supported consequence].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Three fictional pilot teams could not trace claims back to interview notes. Here are the two missing steps: recording the source and checking the wording.
requirements: Support prevalence and consequence; use most only with a suitable denominator. Count real components rather than padding the list. Describe practical stakes without amplifying fear or inventing confusion.

name: Relatable Struggle/Unexpected Truth
template: An easy-to-miss part of [activity] is [supported complication]. Here is when it matters.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: An easy-to-miss part of a summary workflow is checking whether two similar quotes came from different customers. Here is a fictional example.
requirements: Support the complication and its relevance. Do not claim nobody warns readers or that every tool fails. Explain conditions and avoid presenting editorial surprise as a measured audience reaction.

name: Emotion-Driven Pain Point
template: [Only with source-backed writer observations; otherwise label hypothetical] I saw [bounded audience] describe [pain in their own words]. After [change], they reported [supported difference].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I saw a fictional team describe approval handoffs as frustrating. After assigning a reviewer, they reported fewer unanswered status questions.
requirements: Source observation, any emotional wording, baseline, change and reported difference. Do not infer feelings from spend or working hours. Distinguish reported relief from measured savings and avoid unsupported causal claims.

name: Numbers-Driven List/Benefit
template: [Actual count] [resources or methods with a bounded purpose] for [audience], checked in [date or year].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Four interview-review prompts for solo founders, checked in a fictional October 2026 exercise.
requirements: Provide the actual items and match the count. Check relevance and current availability for the stated date. Benefits describe supported uses, not guaranteed productivity or revenue gains. Examples are not evidence of current product behavior.

name: Urgency/Fear of Missing Out
template: [If a real deadline is verified] To [retain specific opportunity], complete [action] by [date], because [documented consequence]. [Otherwise] Before [planned event], consider [preparation] for [supported reason].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Before your planned pilot review, confirm who will check the interview quotes so the team can discuss the evidence together.
requirements: Use urgency only with a real date, source, relevant audience and supported consequence. If those are absent, use the neutral planning variant. Do not invent expiring advantages, guaranteed missed gains or deadlines.

name: Credibility/Social Proof Challenge
template: [Specific dated advice] does not fit [documented current condition]. Here is what [bounded evidence] suggests instead.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: The fictional June checklist assumes one reviewer. The September pilot had three. Its review log shows why named ownership mattered.
requirements: Verify the prior advice, its date, what changed and the comparison evidence. State sample and limits. Do not call an entire industry's advice outdated or imply hundreds of implementations without records.

name: Top 3 Mistakes
template: Three [documented mistakes] to check for when [activity], ranked by [supported criterion if using top].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Three mistakes to check for in an interview summary: missing attribution, merged quotes and unsupported numbers.
requirements: Use only when three distinct mistakes exist and the body explains each. Do not accuse the reader of making them without evidence. Top requires a ranking basis; otherwise present an unranked checklist or choose another hook.

name: Buy/ use This Instead
template: For [specific use case], consider [alternative] instead of [common option], if [fit condition]. Here is the comparison on [criteria].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: For a two-person pilot, consider a shared review sheet instead of a dedicated review platform if you only need an owner and a status field.
requirements: Verify current alternatives, required capabilities, total costs and constraints. Explain tradeoffs. A recommendation does not authorize a purchase or imply that free options meet every team's needs.

name: Speed Tutorial
template: How to [bounded task], explained in [verified reading or viewing duration].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: How to add a source-check column to a review sheet, explained in two minutes.
requirements: Verify the explanation fits the stated duration. Distinguish tutorial length from implementation time or time to business results. Include prerequisites and required human checks.

name: Can’t Believe The Cost
template: [Only with the writer's supplied reaction] I was surprised by [verified price or free tier] for [offer]. Here is what that includes and excludes.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I was surprised by the fictional ReviewPad plan at $8 per user per month. The example price excludes tax and requires annual billing.
requirements: Verify current price, currency, region, account eligibility, billing commitment, taxes or fees and limits before use. Free must identify restrictions. Do not borrow a reaction or publish the synthetic price as a real offer.

name: Cheapest Way
template: A lower-cost way to [goal] than [specified comparator], under [cost assumptions]. [Use lowest-cost only within a verified comparison set].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: A lower-cost way to run this fictional pilot than Plan B is Plan A, if you need only two seats and no paid integrations.
requirements: Compare total cost on equal scope, dates and terms, including labor or setup where material. State the options examined and missing coverage. Never claim universal cheapest from a partial search.

name: Need‑To‑Know Guide
template: What [audience] needs to know about [topic] before [specific decision or activity].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: What a two-person team needs to know about review ownership before starting a shared publishing queue.
requirements: Define audience and decision. Deliver a useful guide covering relevant prerequisites, limits and next steps. Support factual statements and avoid implying comprehensive expertise beyond the covered scope.

name: Wish I Knew Sooner
template: [Only with the writer's supplied retrospective experience; otherwise label hypothetical] Something I wish I had known before [event] is [specific lesson].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Something I wish I had known before my first fictional pilot is that each review request needs a named owner.
requirements: Verify the event, learning and retrospective preference with the writer. Explain the lesson's context. Do not invent regret, biography or a universal maxim.

name: Friendly Warning
template: A caution for [audience] doing [activity]: [supported risk under specific conditions]. Check [practical safeguard].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: A caution for teams sharing customer quotes: a summary can lose the speaker's qualifying words. Check the original passage before publishing.
requirements: Establish the risk mechanism and when it applies. Use current authoritative evidence for product privacy or security claims. Do not claim a tool leaks data solely because it is free. Offer a proportionate safeguard.

name: Before I Started
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] [Actual count] things I wish I had known before I [started or completed activity].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Three things I wish I had known before I completed a fictional review pilot: define the owner, retain the source and record unresolved questions.
requirements: Verify that the writer started or completed the stated activity and supplied these lessons. Match the real count. Keep starting and completion distinct; do not pad the list or invent experience.

name: Too Good To Be True
template: Can [specific claimed benefit] hold up under [test conditions]? Here is [verified result] and where it stops.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Can one prompt produce a review-ready interview summary? In this fictional test it captured the topics but missed a qualifying sentence.
requirements: Pay off the question with a documented test or reliable capability evidence. Preserve limits and failures. Do not inflate the teaser, imply full automation from a partial result or omit the human review required.

name: Truth On Platform
template: What [bounded dated evidence] shows about [topic] on [platform].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: What a fictional review of twelve public posts shows about source links in interview-summary discussions on ExampleForum.
requirements: Verify platform, date, sample and observations. Distinguish platform capability from what users claim. Avoid implied privileged access or an all-encompassing truth based on a narrow sample.

name: Number One For
template: Among [defined options tested], [option] ranked first for [specific criterion] under [conditions].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Among three fictional review layouts, Layout B ranked first for finding the original quote in the timed exercise.
requirements: Define comparison set, criterion, method, date and limits. Support the ranking and report ties or tradeoffs. Do not turn a bounded result into a universal number-one claim.

name: One Thing Rule
template: One useful principle for [goal] is [supported principle]. Start there, while checking [relevant exception or prerequisite].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: One useful principle for reviewing a summary is to keep every quote traceable. You still need to check whether the surrounding context changes its meaning.
requirements: Focus on one defensible principle while naming important limits. Do not claim it is the only thing required, a substitute for expertise or a guarantee of mastery.

name: Can’t Believe These Work
template: [Only with source-backed writer testing and supplied reaction; otherwise label hypothetical] I was surprised that [methods] met [success criterion] in [test]. Here is the result.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I was surprised that a one-page checklist caught all four planted attribution errors in my fictional rehearsal. Here is the test setup.
requirements: Verify personal participation, reaction, test setup, result and success criterion. Include sample limits and failures. Do not borrow surprise or claim general effectiveness from a staged test.

name: Instead, Do This
template: For [specific situation], try [alternative action] instead of [current action], because [supported reason].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: For a draft with missing sources, request the original passages instead of polishing the wording first.
requirements: Support the proposed sequence or substitution and its fit. Explain exceptions, costs and required expertise. Do not imply a tool can replace a worker or entire process without evidence.

name: 5 Tips To Get It
template: Five [substantive tips] for working toward [goal], under [conditions].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Five tips for a clearer fictional interview summary: name speakers, preserve qualifiers, link sources, separate inference and flag open questions.
requirements: Use only if five distinct useful tips exist. Treat the outcome as a goal unless demonstrated. Any deadline or measured gain needs evidence; do not promise instant improvement or pad the list.

name: Did You Know
template: Did you know [sourced and scoped fact]? Here is [brief explanation or demonstration].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Did you know this fictional test summary merged two speakers into one? Here are the two source passages and the resulting sentence.
requirements: Verify the fact with a source and relevant date. Scope capability and performance claims to conditions. Resolve the curiosity promptly; do not invent statistics, speed or conversion lifts.

name: Are You Looking To…
template: Are you [audience] looking to [stated objective]? Here is [specific relevant help].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Are you a solo founder looking to organize your first five customer interviews? Here is a planning checklist.
requirements: Use an audience and objective from the brief or supported research. Offer relevant help without inferring sensitive traits or promising multiplied productivity.

name: If You’re Like Me
template: [Only with source-backed writer habit or experience; otherwise label hypothetical] If you also [specific activity or difficulty I have described], this [resource] may help with [bounded task].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: If you also lose track of which draft needs review, this status-sheet example may help you find the next owner. In this fictional scenario, I had the same problem.
requirements: Verify the writer's habit or experience and avoid inventing reader similarity. The shared difficulty must come from the writer, not a generic persona. Support the resource's intended use without a guaranteed result.

name: Why You Need This
template: Why [audience] may need [resource] when [specific condition applies].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Why a team may need a source log when several reviewers work from the same interview transcript.
requirements: Tie the recommendation to a supported use case and material need. Explain when a simpler alternative suffices. Do not claim necessity for all businesses or audiences.

name: A vs B
template: [Option A] vs [Option B] for [use case]: [bounded verdict on stated criteria].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Fictional Layout A vs Layout B for source review: B needed fewer clicks in the three-task test, while A showed more context.
requirements: Compare actual versions, prices or conditions where relevant. Define criteria, method and limitations. Include material tradeoffs. No always-wins verdict or invented win probability.

name: Legal Hack
template: For [jurisdiction and use case], [method] may reduce [cost] under [verified conditions]. [Only with current legal support: precise applicable legal qualification].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: In a fictional tool comparison, using an eligible community license reduced subscription fees. Eligibility, license duties and migration costs still need review.
requirements: Keep the historical name only; omit hack and legality claims unless justified. Before a legal claim, verify current jurisdiction-specific authoritative support and applicability. Verify license terms, eligibility and total costs. This is not a tax loophole or legal-compliance guarantee.

name: New Cheat Code
template: A [demonstrated method] for [specific task]. [Only if dated evidence supports it: what is newly available or newly tested].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: A review-sheet method for flagging quotes without source links. Here is a worked fictional example.
requirements: Show the method and limits. Verify any novelty date and whose experience is new. Do not imply a secret shortcut, policy bypass or untested productivity gain.

name: Life‑Changer
template: [Method] can help with [bounded supported benefit] under [conditions]. [Use a personal life-change opinion only if the writer supplied and substantiated that experience].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: A named review owner can help a pilot team identify who should respond next. Here is how the fictional handoff works.
requirements: Replace sweeping life-change promises with a specific supported use. If retaining a personal opinion, attribute it to the actual writer and verify the underlying experience. Do not promise the reader the same result.

name: Mind‑Blower
template: Look at [specific demonstrated result] from [method], under [conditions]. Here is how it happened.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Look at the two source passages this fictional review checklist kept separate. The first draft had merged their speakers.
requirements: Provide a real demonstration before claiming a result. Explain conditions and failure cases. Do not dictate the reader's emotional reaction or inflate a limited capability.

name: You Won’t Believe These
template: [Actual count or bounded set] [available items or features] for [specific use], with [verified constraint].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Three fictional review layouts for small teams, each with an owner field and a source-link column.
requirements: Verify the items, availability, versions and any price ceiling as of a date. Deliver the discovery list without predicting disbelief. Do not use the synthetic items or costs as real recommendations.

name: Don’t Want To…
template: Want to reduce [documented hassle]? Try [supported method] when [fit condition].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Want to reduce repeated questions about who reviews next? Try a named-owner column when several people share a queue.
requirements: Confirm the hassle and remedy fit the audience. Support any claimed time or cost reduction with measurements. Include required effort and limits; no guaranteed removal of the problem.

name: Started Sooner
template: [Only with the writer's supplied retrospective preference; otherwise label hypothetical] Something I wish I had started earlier is [practice]. Here is why, in [specific context].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Something I wish I had started earlier in my fictional pilot is keeping a list of unanswered interview questions. It gave each review meeting a starting point.
requirements: Verify the practice, actual start and writer's retrospective preference. Explain the context without inventing regret or implying the practice would have changed past outcomes with certainty.

name: Without vs With
template: [Only with comparable source-backed writer records; otherwise label hypothetical] My [workflow or situation] without [method], compared with after [method]: [documented contrast].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: My fictional review queue before and after adding an owner field: the later version shows who should respond next. The team also changed its meeting schedule.
requirements: Verify participation, comparable periods, scope and contrast. Name confounding changes. A before-and-after comparison does not prove the tool caused time savings, revenue growth or improved life quality.

name: No More Gatekeeping
template: Here is [shareable method or resource], including [useful detail often omitted from the short explanation].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Here is the complete fictional review checklist, including the steps for handling an untraceable quote.
requirements: Confirm permission to share the resource and any underlying examples. Deliver the useful detail. Do not invent a prior agreement, claim secret ownership or imply others deliberately withheld ordinary information.

name: Guess What This Is
template: What produced [specific visible output]? [Prompt reveal of the verified method and conditions].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: What produced this fictional source-check table? A review prompt plus a human check of the original passages.
requirements: Show the object or result and promptly explain its origin. Verify the demonstration and disclose human work. Do not exaggerate capability, conceal material setup or promise disbelief.

name: Best For, Here’s Why
template: [Items] are strong choices for [specific purpose] among [options evaluated], using [criteria]. Here is why, including the tradeoffs.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Layouts A and C are strong choices for source review among the four fictional layouts compared, using link visibility and owner clarity as criteria.
requirements: Define the audience, comparison set, criteria, current evidence and tradeoffs. Best may be used only with an explicit bounded basis. Do not claim universal superiority or conceal suitability limits.

name: First Time Ever
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] I tried [specific activity] for the first time. Here is [documented observation].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I tried a fictional three-person review rehearsal for the first time. Two reviewers interpreted the same status label differently.
requirements: Verify the event occurred and was first for this writer, not first globally. Supply records and actual observations. Do not invent an experiment, profitable launch or unattended automation.

name: Actually Works
template: [Only with source-backed writer trials; otherwise label hypothetical] [Products] I tried that met [specific success criterion] for [use case]. Here are the limits.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Two fictional note tools I tried that preserved source links in the export test. Here are the formats that failed.
requirements: Verify personal participation, products or versions, test criteria and outcomes. Define any best ranking. Include material failures and limits. Do not convert borrowed reviews into first-person endorsement.

name: I Tested Everything
template: [Only with source-backed writer tests; otherwise label hypothetical] I tested [bounded set of options] on [shared task]. Here is what I found.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I tested four fictional writing tools on the same review brief. Here is how each handled missing source links.
requirements: State actual coverage, selection method, versions, dates, conditions and writer participation. Every requires a closed explicitly named universe and verified complete coverage. A bounded test does not replace every reader's own checks.

name: I Sampled It All
template: [Only with source-backed writer sampling; otherwise label hypothetical] I sampled [defined selection] of [offerings]. Here are my picks for [criteria and audience].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I sampled introductory lessons from three fictional review courses. Here are my picks for worked examples, based only on those lessons.
requirements: Verify personal sampling, selection, depth, dates and criteria. Distinguish a sample or free lesson from full use or course completion. Do not claim every offering was sampled unless the closed universe is documented.

name: I Experimented For You
template: [Only with source-backed writer experiments; otherwise label hypothetical] I compared [methods] under [test conditions]. These met [criterion], and these did not.
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I compared three fictional prompt formats on the same six passages. Two kept the speakers separate; one merged a pair.
requirements: Verify participation, methods, shared inputs, repeatability, evaluation criteria and full outcomes. Bound the tested set and report failures. Do not claim the method works generally or that every technique was tried.

name: I Researched It All
template: [Only with source-backed writer research; otherwise label hypothetical] I reviewed [bounded sources or options], spending [auditable time if relevant]. Here is [supported finding].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I reviewed the documentation for five fictional note tools over three recorded hours. Here is what each says about exporting source links.
requirements: Verify participation, research scope, sources, dates and any time log. Distinguish documented capability from hands-on testing. Omit inflated hours, exhaustive claims and best verdicts without evidence.

name: I Found What Works
template: [Only with source-backed writer research and use; otherwise label hypothetical] I researched [bounded methods] and tried [actual subset]. Here is what helped me with [measured task].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: I researched four fictional review routines and tried two. A named-owner step helped me identify the next reviewer in each rehearsal.
requirements: Separate researched methods from tested ones. Verify personal participation, outcome criteria and observations. Bound helped-me claims to the situation and disclose other changes. Do not borrow another person's results.

name: Should Be Illegal
template: A useful result worth examining: [specific supported benefit] from [method], under [conditions].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: A useful result worth examining: this fictional checklist caught four missing citations before the draft reached the editor.
requirements: Keep the historical name only. Remove illegality rhetoric and impossible work-equivalence claims. Verify the result, baseline, method and limits; do not imply unauthorized access or guaranteed full-process automation.

name: My Go‑To
template: [Only with the writer's supplied and source-backed preference; otherwise label hypothetical] My usual [tool or method] for [specific task] is [choice], because [documented reason].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: My usual starting point for a fictional interview review is a source-link table, because it lets me open each quoted passage.
requirements: Verify that the writer actually uses and prefers the choice for this task. Support functional claims and disclose material sponsorship if applicable. No fabricated endorsement or implied universal best option.

name: Before You Scroll
template: Before you scroll, here is [specific useful fact, demonstration or resource] for [relevant task].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Before you scroll, here is a fictional example of a quote whose meaning changes when its final sentence is removed.
requirements: Use only when a concise attention request serves the actual content. Deliver the payoff immediately. Source any savings, revenue or performance claim; do not fabricate stakes to hold attention.

name: Get Rid Of It
template: [Actual count] ways to reduce [specific recurring problem], with [important limit].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Three ways to reduce untraceable quotes: keep source links, retain speaker labels and check exports. Review is still required.
requirements: Give the actual number of substantive methods. Support problem-remedy fit and describe residual risk. Do not promise elimination, guaranteed time savings or a cure. Use another count if only fewer methods are supported.

name: Ordered vs Got
template: [Only with source-backed writer experience; otherwise label hypothetical] What I expected from [order or request], compared with what was delivered: [specific contrast].
example: Synthetic example, not a user fact: Hypothetical comparison: I requested a summary with source links. The delivered example had the topics but omitted three links.
requirements: Verify the order or request, expectation, delivery and writer's participation. Preserve requested and delivered wording where quoted. Label fictional comparisons hypothetical and avoid inventing customer transactions or transformations.

name: Platform Secret
